newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt ends weaker as NZD dips after RBNZ comment.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt ends weaker as NZD dips after RBNZ comment.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.25 (PREV 92.34) 90-DAYS 7.62 (PREV 7.52)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.50 PCT (PREV 7.45) US 5-YR 6.55 (PREV 6.55)
* NZ short end 10 pts higher as Kiwi weakens
* RBNZ's Brash tells FEC Kiwi "somewhat overvalued"
* Dealers expect dollar to rebound overnight, bills to recover
The short end of New Zealand's debt market finished sharply weaker on Wednesday after Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash sent the Kiwi dollar into a dive.

The Kiwi kept weakening steadily in afternoon trade following Brash's appearance before parliament's finance and expenditure committee (FEC), during which he said the dollar appeared "somewhat overvalued".
It ended at US$0.6901/08 and 67.88 on its Trade-Weighted Index, from 0.6940/47 and 68.32 at the open.

Brash said monetary conditions had eased as the bank wanted in the wake of its economic projections released last Thursday. The projections assumed 90-day bank bills at 7.50 percent and the TWI at 68.0 throughout the forecast period.

The 90-days, which were a point weaker at 7.53 percent going into the FEC meeting, ended the session at 7.62 percent. The June futures contract was eight points weaker at 92.25 on good volume of 3,119 contracts traded.

Dealers said Brash had told the markets nothing new but the concerted discussion on the New Zealand dollar continued to push it lower. One said the Kiwi had not looked convincing in early trade before the statement, which had not helped.
"The Kiwi didn't bounce back after last night's sell-off, so the market was a bit nervous on that all day really," he said.
Another dealer said the currency's move lower had the smell of a knee-jerk reaction, and offshore investors tended not to worry themselves over the repetition of remarks like Brash's.

"I would think the Kiwi probably will come back from here overnight. I think they probably sold it more on speculative positions than people getting out. So it's just a matter now whether they decide there's real selling behind it or whether it's people trying to get in front of the sellers."
Dealers said the TWI was beginning to take on significance not seen for a while.

"It's not a one-way bet now and I think people will take a lot more notice of the TWI...Bill rates are going to be much more sensitive and correlated to the TWI than what they have been for the last three or four months," one said.
Volumes were generally quiet in the bond market, although the short end's negative sentiment began to seep into the bonds by the end of the day.
"It's just drifting up a little bit at the close here, purely because the Kiwi's sub-68 on the TWI," one dealer said.
The bonds managed to finish largely flat.
